subject: biology
topicDisplay: Core Concepts Assessed Across All Components
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In eukaryotes, splicing of pre-mRNA involves:
options: Removal of introns and joining of exons
Addition of a poly-A tail only
Translation of the coding sequence
Removal of exons and joining of introns
questions.explain: Splicing removes the non-coding introns and joins the exons together to produce mature mRNA.

questions.q: A substitution mutation in a coding region may have no effect on the polypeptide produced. This is most likely because:
options: The ribosome corrects the error
The degenerate nature of the code means the new codon may still code for the same amino acid
Substitutions always cause a frameshift
The mutation occurs in an intron only
questions.explain: Owing to degeneracy, an altered codon can still specify the same amino acid (a synonymous/silent mutation).

questions.q: The Bohr effect describes how an increase in carbon dioxide (and fall in pH):
options: Shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the left, increasing haemoglobin's affinity
Has no effect on oxygen affinity
Increases the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood
Shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, so haemoglobin releases more oxygen at a given partial pressure
questions.explain: Higher CO2 lowers haemoglobin's oxygen affinity, shifting the curve right so more oxygen is unloaded in respiring tissues.

questions.q: Carbon dioxide is mostly transported in the blood as:
options: Hydrogencarbonate ions formed in red blood cells
Carbonic acid in the plasma
Dissolved CO2 in the plasma
Carbaminohaemoglobin
questions.explain: Most CO2 is converted by carbonic anhydrase in red cells to carbonic acid, which dissociates into hydrogencarbonate ions carried in the plasma.

questions.q: Cellulose differs from starch in that cellulose is composed of:
options: alpha-glucose joined by 1,4 glycosidic bonds
beta-glucose with alternate molecules inverted, joined by 1,4 glycosidic bonds
beta-glucose joined only by 1,6 glycosidic bonds
alpha-glucose with 1,6 branch points
questions.explain: Cellulose consists of beta-glucose monomers, with every other molecule rotated 180 degrees, allowing straight chains and hydrogen bonding between chains.

questions.q: The very large surface area of the small intestine for absorption is produced by:
options: Villi and microvilli on the epithelial cells
Numerous goblet cells secreting mucus
A dense capillary network in the submucosa only
A thick muscular wall
questions.explain: Folded villi each covered in microvilli (the brush border) massively increase the absorptive surface area of the ileum.

questions.q: Insects limit water loss from their tracheal system mainly by:
options: Closing the spiracles using valves and hairs
Increasing ventilation by abdominal pumping
Producing surfactant in the tracheoles
Using haemoglobin to carry oxygen in the blood
questions.explain: Spiracles can be closed by valves, reducing the evaporative water loss that would otherwise occur from the moist tracheal lining.

questions.q: In semi-conservative replication, each new DNA molecule consists of:
options: Two original strands joined together
Fragments of both original strands recombined
One original strand and one new strand
Two newly synthesised strands
questions.explain: Each daughter molecule conserves one parental strand which acts as a template for one newly synthesised strand.

questions.q: At high substrate concentration with fixed enzyme concentration, the rate of reaction plateaus because:
options: the enzyme has denatured
all active sites are occupied so enzyme concentration becomes the limiting factor
the substrate is used up
the pH has changed
questions.explain: When substrate is in excess, every active site is continually occupied, so the number of enzyme molecules limits the rate.

questions.q: On a graph of reaction rate against temperature for a human enzyme, the rate rises to a peak around 37 C then falls sharply. The sharp fall above 40 C is best explained by:
options: a continued increase in kinetic energy
a fall in substrate concentration
an increase in enzyme concentration
denaturation as bonds maintaining the active site break
questions.explain: Beyond the optimum, excessive vibration breaks the hydrogen and ionic bonds holding the tertiary structure, denaturing the active site and sharply reducing activity.

questions.q: The primary structure of a protein refers to:
options: the association of multiple polypeptide subunits
the specific sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide
the overall 3D folding stabilised by R-group interactions
the alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets
questions.explain: Primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids determined by the gene, dictating all higher levels of folding.

questions.q: Fetal haemoglobin has a dissociation curve to the LEFT of adult haemoglobin because:
options: It is less saturated at every partial pressure of oxygen
It carries less oxygen overall
It must release oxygen more readily to the placenta
It has a higher affinity for oxygen, allowing it to load oxygen from maternal blood at the placenta
questions.explain: A higher oxygen affinity (curve to the left) lets fetal Hb take up oxygen from maternal Hb across the placenta.
